paras: The Ninth Street riot was a gunfight between an armed crowd of Black men and a party of white men in Wilmington, Delaware, on the night of June 25, 1903, three days after a white mob burned George White at the stake. Two policemen and at least two Black men were wounded, and two Black men were clubbed, arrested and sentenced the next day. A Black man, William Kramer, was fatally shot nearby the same night in a killing a coroner's jury laid to another Black man.

George White, accused of murdering Helen Bishop, had been burned at the stake, and on the night of June 24 a white mob held the streets and repeatedly attacked Black residents. According to the New York Sun, Black men armed themselves the next day to resist such attacks, and dealers reported their stocks of firearms exhausted.

About 8 p.m. a crowd of Black men, about 200 by the Delaware account, gathered at Ninth and Walnut streets with clubs, marched along Ninth Street and knocked down a white man and a boy. Shortly before 11 p.m. a party of white men met the crowd near King Street. The Sun wrote that nobody knew which side began it, while police-side accounts said a Black man slapped a white man named Chamberlain and the Black men opened fire, after which white men answered with revolvers.

Sergeant Eugene McDermott went for Leander Moore, who held a revolver; Moore fired, and McDermott and Patrolman Francis Green were wounded in the face before Moore was clubbed into submission. Green seized Joseph S. Shockley, and the Sun reported that police gave both men "a sound clubbing." James A. Mercer, a Black man in the crowd, was wounded in the scalp, and the Evening Star reported a second Black man shot.

Around midnight, near the Pennsylvania Railroad station in the Black district called "the coast," William Kramer was shot in the stomach and died early the next morning. The Evening World reported that William Simms, a Black man from Tarrytown, New York, confessed to shooting Kramer after an insult.

On June 26 Judge Cochran of the City Court sentenced Moore to one year and fined Shockley $50 and costs, on charges reported variously as inciting to riot, assault and battery, and disorderly conduct. Arthur Corwell, the only man arrested in the White lynching, was discharged the same day. A coroner's jury found that Kramer died of a wound inflicted by Simms, and a jury for Simms's murder trial was drawn on September 28; no report of the verdict was found.

Governor John Hunn met with judges and city officials, who reportedly decided to make no more arrests until feeling subsided. The mayor asked parents to keep children home, and the Tribune reported white boys with rifles staging "a miniature hunt for negroes."

On June 26 a short wire report ran from Indianapolis to Kalispell and Pine Bluff, beside longer dispatches from New York correspondents. The wire quoted the marchers' leaders as saying they "do not intend to quietly submit to such abuse." White framing otherwise cast the Black crowd as the aggressor: the Kalispell Bee's headline spoke of a "Bloodthirsty Contingent of Coons," the Alexandria Gazette of "turbulent negroes," and the Evening World of "NEGRO RIOTERS QUICKLY PUNISHED."

The Tribune called the marchers "the lowest element of the colored population" but next day set their sentences against Corwell's discharge. Only the Sun explained the arming as defense against the previous night's mob, and a later Tribune feature in mocking dialect blamed the fracas on a white man's remark.

The Black press carried the riot late and briefly. The Professional World ran the wire copy on July 3 under "DELAWARE SCENE OF TROUBLE," and the Baltimore Afro-American gave the sentences two lines in a news digest. The Colored American printed a Wilmington report on the inquest and a sermon urging moderation, and Paul Laurence Dunbar, in the Topeka Plaindealer, named Wilmington among that summer's race riots.

On who shot Kramer, first-night reports blamed an unknown white man and the Washington Times thought a Black man fired; the later local reports, the confession and the coroner's verdict, the better evidence, named Simms.

reader.title: Ninth Street riot (Wilmington, Delaware, 1903)
bases: A street clash between an armed Black crowd and white men on Ninth Street, in which shots were exchanged on both sides and police clubbed and arrested two Black men, followed by a separate fatal shooting that the inquest attributed to a Black man (A2, A7, A18, A21); neither a lynching nor a one-sided white attack on a Black community.

Independent reports (the Tribune's and the Evening World's own correspondents, the Sun, the Associated wire, and the Delaware Middletown Transcript) agree on the Ninth Street clash, the wounding of McDermott and Mercer, and the arrest and sentencing of Moore and Shockley (A1, A2, A9, A10, A18); who shot Kramer is contested (A1, A21).

accounts.label: First wire report
accounts.gist: About 200 Black men marching on Ninth Street were challenged by about 25 white men and over 100 shots were exchanged; elsewhere Cramer was shot in the stomach by a white man.

accounts.label: Police-side local narrative
accounts.gist: A Black crowd with clubs knocked down white pedestrians, a Black man slapped or stabbed a white man, the Black men began shooting crying 'Let's clean the corner,' whites retaliated, and Moore fired at McDermott and hit Green.

accounts.label: The Sun's correspondent
accounts.gist: Black men had armed to resist attacks made on them the night before; when a party of white men met them, nobody knew who began it, and the police clubbed Moon and Shockley.

accounts.label: Second-day wire and coroner's jury
accounts.gist: Kramer was killed in a fight among Black men by William Simms, who was held for murder; the coroner's jury found Simms inflicted the wound.

accounts.label: Crowd leaders
accounts.gist: The leaders of the marchers said they meant to resent attacks made on their race the night before, would not submit to abuse, and had no sympathy for White.

framing.detail: The Alexandria Gazette opened with police 'quelling an outbreak of turbulent negroes', and the Kalispell Bee's headline spoke of a 'Bloodthirsty Contingent of Coons'.

The Tribune's correspondent called the marchers 'the lowest element of the colored population' and described a 'reign of terror', but next day set the Black men's sentences against the discharge of the only lynching suspect.
The Sun said Black men had armed to resist the previous night's attacks and that 'Which began it nobody quite knows'.
The Evening World headlined 'NEGRO RIOTERS QUICKLY PUNISHED', and a later Tribune feature retold the night in mocking dialect.

The Professional World and the Baltimore Afro-American printed wire copy and a court item without comment; the Colored American carried a delayed Wilmington report on the inquest and a sermon urging moderation.
